cues.text: Homesick
Didier Drogba was born in 1978 in Abidjan, in Ivory Coast.
When he was five, his parents sent him to France to live with his uncle, Michel Goba, who was a professional footballer.
It was a long way from home, and Didier became homesick.
Fly the plane home.
After three years, he went back to Abidjan.
There, he played football every day in a car park in the city.
His mum even gave him a nickname: Tito.
Missing home is a real feeling, and it’s okay to say so. Telling people how you feel helps them help you.
Together again
But his time back home was short.
Both of his parents lost their jobs, so Didier went back to France to live with his uncle again.
Many children would find it hard to move away from their parents a second time.
Slide the family together.
In 1991 his parents came to France too, first to Vannes, and in 1993 they settled in Antony.
At fifteen, Didier moved back in with his parents, brothers and sisters.
The family was together again.
When money is tight or plans change, families can still stick together. Better days can come.
A late start
In Antony, Didier joined a local youth team, and then a club called Levallois.
He scored lots of goals for the youth team, and he even scored on his first-team debut.
But the first-team coach was not impressed.
Didier had never been to a football academy.
He only began training every day as a grown-up, at Le Mans, where he also studied at university.
At first he kept getting injured.
Stack the four blocks.
His coach later said it took Didier four years to be able to train every day and play every week.
Starting later than others is okay. Progress takes time, so keep building, one day at a time.
Patience pays off
By twenty-one, Didier knew he had to become a professional soon, or he might never get the chance.
In 1999 he signed his first professional contract, and his son Isaac was born.
Didier later said Isaac’s birth was a turning point in his life.
There were more setbacks.
He got injured, lost his place, and then struggled to score.
At Guingamp, the coaches were unsure about him, but they were patient.
Pass the ball to Didier.
The next season he scored 17 goals, and he praised his teammates, like his old friend Florent Malouda.
Setbacks happen to everyone. Patience, and good teammates, can help you through them.
A wish for peace
For five years, there was a civil war in Didier’s home country, Ivory Coast.
On 8 October 2005, the national team beat Sudan and qualified for their first ever World Cup.
In the changing room, Didier spoke to the TV cameras.
He asked the people who were fighting to put down their weapons.
Unfold the peace banner.
His plea was answered with a ceasefire.
Later, he helped move a big match to the city of Bouaké, which helped the peace process.
Your voice matters. Speaking up kindly, for peace and for others, can help more than you know.
Giving back
In 2007 the United Nations made Didier a Goodwill Ambassador.
In 2010, Time magazine named him one of the world’s 100 most influential people, because of his part in the peace process.
In 2009 he gave three million pounds from an advertising deal to build a hospital in his hometown, Abidjan, through his own foundation.
He decided to do it after visiting other hospitals there.
Build the hospital.
The homesick boy from Abidjan had come home to help.
When you’ve been through hard times, you can help others through theirs. Giving back makes everyone stronger.
